findings.title: Negative offset slicing is unsupported by Django and the 'advanced' path is a client-controlled bypass
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` taken from the client-supplied cursor. Django querysets raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for negative slice bounds, so any request with a negative offset becomes a 500. The comments claim the ORM 'properly handles' this and that it 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds', which is wrong and describes a boundary bypass. The path is also enabled by a client-controlled `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter.

findings.title: BasePaginator now passes negative offsets through for prev cursors
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` means that for `is_prev` cursors the raw, possibly negative offset reaches `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Cursor.from_string accepts negative ints, so a user can craft `0:-5:1` and trigger an assertion error (500) on every endpoint using BasePaginator or its subclasses. Before this change the code sliced `[offset:stop]`, which behaved no differently for negative values, but the added comment now claims this is a deliberate, safe feature. The change also affects all callers, not just audit logs.

findings.title: User-controlled flag selects an experimental paginator on a sensitive endpoint
findings.body: The audit-log endpoint switches to OptimizedCursorPaginator when `optimized_pagination=true` and the user is a superuser or has global access. This is an undocumented, unfeatured switch that exposes the unsafe negative-offset path. `request.user.is_superuser` is checked without verifying an active superuser session. The comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' does not justify skipping bounds checks. There is also no test coverage for this branch.

findings.title: New paginator duplicates BasePaginator logic and has no tests
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator copy-pastes nearly all of BasePaginator.get_result, and its get_item_key is the plain integer version rather than the datetime version. When used with `order_by="-datetime"` in the audit-log endpoint, `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError, so the optimized path crashes on the first page. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw int, which is then compared against a datetime column. No tests were added.

findings.title: Redirect-depth loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without justification
findings.body: The loop bound was lowered from 10000 to 1000, and the comment about depth limits was removed. Segment trees deeper than 1000 will no longer have their redirects resolved correctly, so their spans end up in the wrong set. This is unrelated to the eviction change and unexplained.

findings.title: Span count check removed from load path; max_segment_spans now unused
findings.body: The `max_segment_spans` check in `_load_segment_data` was deleted, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now dead. The Lua script hardcodes 1000, which is inconsistent with the default of 1001. Eviction in Lua is also not covered by any test (no test inserts more than 1000 spans). The module docstring still says sets, not sorted sets.

findings.title: end_timestamp_precise accessed with hard indexing
findings.body: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises KeyError if a span lacks the field, which crashes the whole batch in the consumer (poison message). Previously, spans without it were processed fine. A fallback or validation is needed. In addition, zadd with the scores gives spans identical payloads the same member, so dedup semantics stay the same, but eviction (zpopmin) drops the oldest spans, which may include the root span.
